## Overview

Koreans are an East Asian ethnic group indigenous to the Korean Peninsula. Most Koreans live in the two sovereign states of North and South Korea, collectively referred to as Korea, while communities also live in China, Japan, Kazakhstan, Russia, Uzbekistan, Germany, the United Kingdom, France, the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand. In 2021, an estimated 7.3 million ethnic Koreans lived outside Korea. The Korean language belongs to the distinct Koreanic family and uses Hangul as its main writing system. Korean origins remain debated: archaeological evidence connects Proto-Koreans with Manchuria during the Bronze Age, while other interpretations emphasize continuity on the Korean Peninsula. The Korean Peninsula contains the world's largest concentration of dolmens, with an estimated 35,000–100,000 examples.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

Archaeological evidence associates the origins of early Koreans with the Bronze Age dagger culture, which expanded from the West Liao River region. The sources also describe connections between pottery-making styles of Late Neolithic to Bronze Age cultures in the West Liao River basin and the Korean Peninsula.

## Oral tradition & literature

The sources describe genealogical memory and the formation of family narratives rather than a distinct oral literary genre. Korea Foundation Associate Professor of History Eugene Y. Park stated that many Koreans appear to have a genealogical memory blackout before the twentieth century and that the vast majority do not know their actual genealogical history. During the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, families developed master narratives explaining the history of surname and ancestral-seat combinations. A document from 1873 recorded three children in one family, while a later document from 1920 recorded an additional son.

## Language & religion

The language of the Korean people is Korean, which belongs to the distinct Koreanic family according to the source. Hangul, invented by Sejong the Great, is its principal writing system. Hanja has largely been phased out of daily use on the Korean Peninsula, although some South Korean newspapers and media companies use it when referring to key politicians or certain countries. Hanja remains used for academic, historical, and religious purposes. The Roman alphabet functions as a secondary writing system in South Korea, particularly for loanwords, and is widely used in daily and official communication.
